extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians and humor writers (writers who need help with idea generation, joke craft, and revision)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical workbook for generating, developing, and revising stand-up jokes, bits, and longer humorous essays/storytelling, emphasizing daily practice, freewriting, topic exploration, joke structure, and persona. Focused on the writing process rather than stage technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather supplies
rubrics_metrics.description: Essentials: Notebook and pens. Your notebook can (and should) be as cheap as possible. A cheap spiral notebook makes the writing a lot less precious, and you're free to write more crap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other helpful stuff: highlighters, pocket-sized notebooks, index cards, tape recorder, video recorder, thesaurus, dictionary, computer, internet, newspapers, reference books, filing system, computer word processor, printer, calendar. Recommendation: consider Scrivener for organization. Cheap notebook reduces pressure ("I will not buy a Moleskine... I can’t handle the pressure.").

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan to write / Set a schedule and goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a writing schedule and stick to it. Set reasonable goals: one 10-minute freewrite every morning, 10 bad jokes a day, 3 pages a day, a new 5-minute set every 2 weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that most first drafts are awful; commit to writing daily (even 10 minutes). Book a gig or sign up for a deadline to force production. Put writing times in your calendar, highlight them, and protect that time. Don't do chores or check phone—just sit and write garbage if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep everything; don't throw anything away
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't throw anything away. Bad jokes can turn into good jokes, but only if you write them down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry a small notebook or use your phone to capture half-baked ideas, shoddy premises, news items, observations, strange things people said or did. If you have an idea, no matter how stupid, write it down before you lose it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freewriting / Kill the censor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use freewriting to muffle/kill your internal censor: set a timer and write nonstop for a set time, not editing or judging. The goal is process, not product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules: keep your hand moving, don't stop or edit, don't reread, avoid grammar and punctuation concerns. Typical session: 10 minutes or three pages. Freewriting clears mental clutter and can either lead into a good idea or free space for creative thought. Draws on Julia Cameron's 'morning pages', Natalie Goldberg and Peter Elbow advice: be specific, lose control, don't think, go for first thoughts, repeat words if stuck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freewriting anti-rules (what to avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: During freewriting, do not try to be funny, do not judge, and don't feel the need to form sentences or 'setup-punch' at first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be messy, be boring, be mean. Don't cross out. Don't reread immediately (unless highlighting interesting bits). The goal is to get past the censor, so allow yourself to write the worst junk in America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find your comedy topics (topic generation prompts)
rubrics_metrics.description: All comedy will be about you and the things around you. Start making lists of subjects to write about by answering prompts (What do you love? What do you hate? What are you ashamed of? What are you good at?) and creating a large idea inventory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List at least 10 answers for each question. Do an exercise: make a list of 100 things using prompts (food, appearance, dreams, politics, pets, etc.). Use topic lists to pull random subjects for 2-minute freewriting sprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore a comedy topic (research, brainstorm, organize)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you pick a topic with potential, expand it: list factual statements, research (for public figures), free associate, mind-map, and ask questions (who/what/where/when/why/how) to find what is interesting or funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize by breaking topic into groups/subgroups: classify/divide, causes/effects, similarities/opposites, problem/solution, comparisons, underlying assumptions, logical flaws, contrary points of view. Explore specific people (phrases, habits, hopes). Play 'what if?' and look for extreme cases. Search for Play On Word (POW) opportunities: clichés, double entendres, homonyms, malapropisms, literal takes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find your point of view (POV) and attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine your POV/angle on the topic: what do you want to prove, predict, or recommend? What attitude/emotion do you bring to it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List possible attitudes/emotions (affectionate, ironic, angry, embarrassed, etc.) and tag notebook items with emotional labels. Consider why you feel that way and how it affects the material. A clear, strong POV helps shape premise and punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand what makes people laugh (theories/elements of humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of humor mechanisms: surprise, feeling superior, instinct, incongruity, ambivalence, release, puzzle-solving, familiarity, extremes, shock, silliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mel Helitzer's elements (T–Target, H–Hostility, R–Realism, E–Exaggeration, E–Emotion, S–Surprise) and Scott Adams' '2-of-6 rule' (at least two of Cute/Naughty/Bizarre/Clever/Recognizable/Cruel) are offered as practical checks: identify which elements your material hits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup/punch structure (basic joke architecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jokes have a setup or premise that builds tension and anticipation with an attitude and POV, and then a punchline/twist/payoff that surprises or releases that tension: Setup --> Punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good setup is NOT funny; it's factually true, has a clear emotion, and is specific, visual, and clear. Keep setups short (preferably less than one typewritten line; no longer than two). Bad premises are too long, unclear, preposterous, or contain too many topics before the punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup qualities checklist (clarity, specificity, single subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the premise has only one subject (do not go off on tangents). Is the premise original? Does it fit the audience's emotional needs and humanity?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Is it clear, concise, and concrete? Can you be more visual or understandable? Is the premise ambiguous—can you be more specific? Use active, not passive voice. Cut excess beats and words. Make feeling and attitude clear; strengthen POV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Punch should be a brief surprise with the funniest bit at the very end and usually involve an attitude shift. The audience should be surprised and recognize the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect the surprise (don't give it away); show, don't tell; consider whether the funny part is actually the premise (flip setup and punch if needed). Make the last word as funny as possible; use thesaurus to refine. Consider wordplay, act-outs, and tangents. Trim words aggressively so punch lands cleanly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible setup→punch structures (templates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common relational structures between setup and punch (many from Judy Carter): Information → Exaggeration; Information → Sarcasm; Information → Radical understatement; Word → Unexpected Definition; Question → Offbeat Answer; Question → Absurdity; Theme → Specific example; Sane → Insane; Realistic → Fantasy; Adult view → Child’s view; Friendly → Hostile; Fact → Fiction; Normal → Loony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these templates to generate variations; many successful jokes follow these underlying structure types even when disguised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to punch (techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques for delivering a punch: analogies, 'what ifs', antonyms, double entendres, exaggeration, distortions, funny sounds, homonyms, incongruity, juxtaposition, malapropisms, mangled clichés, metaphors, parodies, sarcasm, satire, shock, similes, surprises, synonyms, triples, using the familiar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick multiple techniques and test combinations; some techniques (shock, cruelty) may require higher skill and audience calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke formulas and templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Stock formulas used in monologues/roasts: '______ is so _____ that ______'; '_______ is almost like _______. The only difference is ________'; 'You know you’re _______ when ____'; '_____ is like _____'; '____ is the only _______ that ________'; '_____ is worse than _____.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formulas to produce material quickly; you can disguise the formula later. They are a tool for productivity, not theft of voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other comedic devices and devices list
rubrics_metrics.description: Other devices include understatement, standard references, compare/contrast, reverses, analogies, paired elements, wordplay (synonyms/antonyms/homonyms), triples (setup/anticipation/punch), realism, transformation/mixes, funny words, foul language, similes, observations, mimicking, reforming clichés, list making, callbacks, shifting attitudes, reflecting truth, release of tension, attacking authority, involving the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider which devices suit your voice and the audience. Avoid relying on any single device exclusively; combine for richer jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision checklist (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: If jokes don't get laughs, revise. Ask: Is the premise original? Single subject? Clear, concise, concrete? Grammar and voice fixed? Premise ambiguous? Strong attitude/POV? Did you give the punch away? Did you offend or alienate the audience?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform live tests (open-mic) and iterate. Try material multiple times before declaring it dead (or that the audience sucks). Cut excess words; aim for active verbs; rework clumsy or clichéd phrases; get feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision checklist (punch-focused)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus revision on punch placement and wording: is the funniest bit the final word? Is there a clear attitude shift? Is the audience surprised and do they recognize the truth?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider flipping setup and punch, change last word, use thesaurus to hunt punchier word, look for wordplay opportunities, act-outs, and tighten wording until punch lands cleanly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterate on strong laughs or failures
rubrics_metrics.description: When you get a big laugh, examine subject and attitude and write more. If you get no laugh, analyze subject and attitude and either change subject or choose a stronger attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wring topics for everything they’re worth: revisit exploration techniques, freewrite, brainstorm more tangents. Keep performing promising material to expand on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop your comic persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Persona emerges over time but should interact with material and audience; a comedian is 'A person with a Problem' and creates 'Joyous Communication.' Successful comedians tend to be: Original, Likeable, Vulnerable, Genuine, Vivid, Charismatic, and Just Plain Funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on being lovable via your struggle, be genuine (reflect and exaggerate off truth), be vivid and clear, and infuse communication with emotions that make the audience comfortable. Persona shapes choices of topics, attitudes, and word choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous essays and storytelling rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For print/storytelling formats: 'Show, don't tell.' Be specific about topic (write about a particular day or incident). Target a specific audience and purpose; have a clear thesis/point that should be evident by the last line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style should be your voice but consider audience. Use fiction/poetry tools (plot, character, setting, dialog, metaphor, rhythm). Organize with a clear beginning, middle, end. Include abundant detail in first draft ('kitchen sink'), then cut ruthlessly in revision. Read aloud, get feedback, and prefer strong verbs over adjectives.
